page: Amazon Web Services t3a.xlarge is a burstable performance instance powered by an AMD EPYC 7571 processor. Built on the x86_64 architecture, this instance features 4 vCPUs mapped to 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. It includes 16.0 GB of DDR4 memory operating at 3 GHz, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. The instance runs on the Nitro hypervisor, lacks local storage, and has a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

Benchmark data indicates that the t3a.xlarge operates primarily in the lower performance tiers. In stress-ng CPU tests, both single-core and multi-core metrics fall into the bottom 10%. Memory bandwidth tests show weak performance, with read-only large block speeds at 23.87 GB/sec and write large block speeds at 11.7 GB/sec. Cryptographic performance is a relative strength, with the PassMark CPU encryption test achieving an average rating of 3207.35. However, database operations and Redis SET operations remain in the bottom 10%.

The burstable CPU allocation model of the t3a.xlarge makes it a cost-efficient option for workloads with variable CPU utilization. Because it relies on CPU credits to handle spikes, it is not suited for sustained high-compute tasks, as reflected in its poor multi-threaded decompression and software compilation benchmarks. This instance is best suited for low-traffic web serving, small-scale development environments, background scripting, or microservices that require moderate memory capacity but experience intermittent CPU demand.
description: Amazon Web Services t3a.xlarge is a burstable general-purpose instance featuring 4 vCPUs and 16.0 GB of DDR4 memory. Powered by an AMD EPYC 7571 processor running at 2.2 GHz on the Nitro hypervisor, it utilizes an x86_64 architecture with 2 physical cores and hyper-threading. The instance lacks local storage and provides a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps. Performance benchmarks place the t3a.xlarge in the lower tiers, with stress-ng CPU and Geekbench multi-core scores falling in the bottom 10%. However, it demonstrates average performance in PassMark CPU encryption tests. Given its burstable CPU allocation and qualitative cost efficiency, this instance is designed for workloads with variable resource demands. It is suited for light web serving, development environments, and background tasks rather than sustained compute-heavy applications.
